sn12.1:1.1: For an overview of this topic, see my Introduction to the Saṁyutta Nikāya.
sn12.1:1.3: In a shift from the previous book, there is no interaction or dialogue; the teaching is a direct address by the Buddha.
sn12.1:1.7: Dependent origination has certain points in common with Vedic cosmogenesis, where the individuation of “name and form” is driven by desire, forged by heat from primordial darkness cloaked in mystery (Rig Veda 3.38, 10.90, 10.121, 10.129). It is deliberately obscured by poets who protect the truth by hiding the highest names (10.5). Such cosmologies were developed in the later stages of the Rig Veda, and further in certain Upaniṣads.
sn12.1:2.1: Most of these terms are pre-Buddhist. In the next discourse we see how the Buddha redefined them to his purpose. Here I give some pre-Buddhist usages to better understand the context.
sn12.1:2.2: “Knowledge” (_veda_) was that of the immortal gods, so knowledge itself is immortal, while ignorance (_avijjā_), being perishable, traps the fool in suffering for life after life. Knowledge and ignorance are part of the mortal condition (Atharva Veda 11.8.23). “A man crosses death through ignorance and attains immortality through knowledge” (Īśa Upaniṣad 11; cf. Paiṅgala Upaniṣad 2.11, Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.1, Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.9).
sn12.1:2.3: “Choices” (_saṅkhāra_) fundamentally means to “construct” or “energize” (Sanskrit _samaskurva_, _saṁskāra_). It is used for the “reviving” or “rejuvenation” of the god Pajāpati when he is depleted by the act of creation, like a fire run low or a man after sex (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 7.2.1.5 *et passim*). The sacrificer thereby perpetuates the creative process, building a new self or body (10.4.1.2). The ritual is “performed” by body, speech, and mind in full awareness (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.16.2–3). Thus the creative act became determined by moral “choices”: a person becomes something good by good deeds, bad by bad deeds (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5).
sn12.1:2.4: “Consciousness” (_viññāṇa_) means to “know clearly, understand”, and hence the sense of awareness that is conscious of whatever happens. The “self” is the Person made of consciousness (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.16). One who is dying abandons the body and senses, becoming one with consciousness, embraced by previous knowledge and actions (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2). They reach out to a new life and become established there, like a caterpillar moving from one leaf to the next.
sn12.1:2.5: “Name and form” (_nāmarūpa_) are the means by which we identify a person of such and such name and appearance (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7). The world manifests as name, form, and action (1.6.1). A virtuous man abandons his old form and fashions a better one as a god, etc. (4.4.4). As the rivers lose their individual names and forms when they enter the ocean, the liberated soul merges with the great Person (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.8, Praśna Upaniṣad 6.5).
sn12.1:2.6: A “field” (_āyatana_) is an “abode” or “proper place” in which one is at rest and safe. Senses are treated unsystematically—the order and number varies, and they are mixed with other things. Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.5.20, for example, says when a man sleeps, he no longer thinks, tastes, smells, sees, or hears. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.1 speaks of inadequate (“one-footed”) manifestations of Divinity: speech, breath, eye, ear, mind (_mano_), heart.
sn12.1:2.14: There is no corresponding “dependent cessation”. The ending of dependent origination is Nibbana, extinguishment.
